rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify limiting peak pairs while aiming for a short run. A midpoint temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to measure the limiting pairs' response to slope. The shallower gradient should spread the central cluster while likely keeping the last peak within 10 minutes.

The limiting pair improves strongly with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the added retention time and keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Injection 3 reached the maximum CRF. Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving its gradient slope to seek a shorter fully resolved separation; the early pair has substantial resolution margin.

Return to the fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test whether retention can be shortened while maintaining the maximum CRF. Changing only temperature isolates its effect on the limiting pair's selectivity.

The central cluster appears to have changed elution order at 50 C; a further temperature increase may separate the crossed pair while shortening retention. Keep the gradient fixed to assess this selectivity change and watch the narrowing earlier pair.
Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the newly limiting pair at 55 C. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving room to recover full resolution without a time penalty.
Use a slope between injections 6 and 7 to shorten the fully resolved 55 C separation. This should retain R above 1.5 for both limiting pairs while bringing the last peak to approximately 9 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping approximately the successful slope of injection 8 to seek a shorter separation. This tests whether the central pairs retain full resolution; the first pair still has some margin against early-peak compression.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a steeper gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method. The temperature series suggests crossings within the central cluster, so cooling may open a different useful separation window.

Test a steep gradient at the highest temperature for a substantially faster separation. The pair approaching co-elution at 55 C may reverse order and reopen, but this run will check whether that creates a useful selectivity window.

Test whether a steeper gradient opens the reversed limiting pair at 60 C while further shortening the run. Keep the starting composition unchanged to preserve early retention, and check for compression of the other central pairs.

Test an intermediate-temperature, higher-starting-organic method for a faster separation. Compared with 55–60 C, cooling should improve early-pair resolution, while the shifted gradient window may separate the central cluster differently.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve separation of the earlier central pair, while steepening the gradient to shorten retention. At 55 C this may balance both limiting pairs better than raising the starting organic fraction did.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 14 to bring its sole limiting pair above R = 1.5. This should keep the last peak near 8 minutes, potentially yielding a faster maximum-CRF method than injection 8.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 15 to shorten the separation while targeting full resolution of both limiting pairs. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Test the unmeasured 35 C selectivity window with a faster gradient than the fully resolved 40 C method. This intermediate temperature may separate the central cluster without the near-co-elution observed at 30 C.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the earlier limiting pair, paired with a steeper slope to reduce total retention. This tests whether the successful 55 C separation can be shortened further while keeping both central pairs above R = 1.5.

Explore the remaining low-temperature selectivity window with a higher starting organic fraction to limit retention. Cooling below the crossings seen at 30–35 C may reopen the central pairs and reveal another fully resolved method.

Probe the untested 45 C selectivity window with a short gradient to look for a faster fully resolved separation. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this run tests an alternative rather than replacing the successful 55 C method.

Test a modestly steeper version of injection 18 to locate the shortest fully resolved boundary at 55 C. The earlier central pair may fall below R = 1.5, but the successful 7.60-minute method remains available.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 50 C separates the crossed central pair while retaining enough resolution in the earlier cluster. This targets a substantially shorter alternative, with injection 18 already providing the maximum CRF.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 15 to improve the earlier limiting pair while retaining separation of the later pair. This targets a maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin than the fastest successful run and a last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Trim injection 18's gradient endpoint while preserving its starting composition and slope. The estimated last-peak elution composition is about 0.57, so all peaks should remain within the gradient and retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed ramp.

Use the final injection to test the resolution boundary between injections 14 and 16, targeting a last peak around 7.6 minutes. The earlier limiting pair may fall just below R = 1.5; injections 18 and 24 remain proven maximum-CRF methods.
